title: Washing feet

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sermon on the Mount: love your enemies. Your line was even them. Did you manage to wish that difficult person one good thing? Today, love you can see, and smell, and get wet from. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

A towel, a basin, some water. That's the whole scene's equipment. It's the last supper Jesus shares with his friends before his arrest, in John's Gospel, and the room is full of people who have walked dusty roads in sandals. Partway through the meal, he gets up. He takes off his outer garment, ties the towel around his waist, pours water into the basin, and kneels in front of the first pair of feet. The room goes quiet. One of them is about to object, loudly. Today: washing feet.
screen: `A TOWEL, A BASIN, SOME WATER.` → `HE GETS UP FROM SUPPER.` → `HE KNEELS AT THEIR FEET.`

segments.voice: John opens the scene with one sentence about love: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Then, instead of a speech, a chore. First, whose job this was. When Abigail agrees to marry David in First Samuel, she says, "let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." In her words, washing feet is the task of a servant who serves the servants. Second, Peter. He can't stand it. "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter, being Peter, swings all the way the other way: then not just my feet, but my hands and my head. Letting yourself be served turns out to be its own kind of humility. Third, who gets washed. The text says Jesus knew who would betray him, and readers notice that no one is skipped. Judas's feet were in that room too. Fourth, the instruction. When he sits back down, he says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." And: "I have given you an example." Churches take that in different ways. Some churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican among them, wash feet in a service on the Thursday before Easter. Some smaller churches wash feet together whenever they share communion. Others read it as a picture of everyday service rather than a rite. The gesture at the center stays the same: love that kneels down.
screen: `A SERVANT'S JOB.` · `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.` · `NO ONE IS SKIPPED.` · `I HAVE GIVEN YOU AN EXAMPLE.` · then, large: `WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look down at your own feet for a moment. Then let a person come to mind whom you could serve today in a small, low, unglamorous way. Not a grand gesture. The dishes no one wants. Taking out their trash. Carrying the heavy bag. Covering the boring shift. Picture yourself doing it without announcing it. Then notice: is there someone you've refused to let serve you? If you pray, you can bring both to God in a few plain words. The bell holds the time.
Washing feet. In John's Gospel, Jesus takes a servant's job at his last supper and tells his friends to do the same for one another. Today's word.
Your line: wash feet. Today, do the low job you pictured for someone, quietly, and don't mention it. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and some other churches hold a foot-washing on the Thursday before Easter, and some smaller churches wash one another's feet as part of communion.

notes: The script quotes John 13:8 as one KJV quote with 'Jesus answered him' inside; in the voice the two halves are split with narration. Confirm.
'Judas's feet were in that room too': John 13:10–11 implies he was washed ('ye are clean, but not all'); framed as what readers notice. Confirm.
'Washing feet belongs to servants' is supported here only by 1 Samuel 25:41 and Peter's reaction; confirm acceptable.
Churches named for Holy Thursday foot-washing (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican) and 'some smaller churches' at communion (e.g. Brethren, some Baptists, Seventh-day Adventists); confirm.
The closing line (love that kneels down) is an interpretive summary; soften if a Keeper prefers.
The jug and the setting 'last supper' are from John 13:2–5 ('supper', 'bason'); the jug is narrative color.
Editor: cut unsourced 'feet were the low job, the one you handed down'; servant claim now rests on Abigail's words only; softened the church list; varied the prayer line.
Audit: cut the invented jug (John 13:5 has only water poured into a basin).
